summary.text: A 54-year-old man weighing 164 kg and measuring 170 cm (BMI 56.75 kg/m²), blood group O Rh-negative, was referred to the Plastic Surgery Department for a massive abdominal pannus that impeded his eligibility for renal transplantation. His medical history included controlled systemic arterial hypertension and ESRD managed with thrice-weekly hemodialysis via a right upper-extremity arteriovenous fistula, as well as severe abdominal lipodystrophy and symptomatic panniculopathy. No medication allergies were documented.

Examination showed a markedly globose abdomen with a large ptotic pannus, significant cutaneous laxity and extensive lipodystrophy, an everted and lateralized umbilicus and a 13-cm surgical scar in the right hypochondrium; the pannus interfered with hygiene and mobility. Preoperative laboratory values included hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, glucose 112 mg/dL (slightly elevated), urea 58.3 mg/dL and creatinine 8.3 mg/dL (markedly increased) and sodium 131 mmol/L (mildly decreased). No preoperative imaging was reported and no abdominal hernias were documented.

After a multidisciplinary assessment, nephrology judged the patient clinically stable for surgery. Under general anesthesia he underwent extended panniculectomy with en-bloc resection of excess skin, subcutaneous tissue and the umbilicus, yielding a 10-kg specimen, rectus muscle plication, two Blake drains and layered closure. A fibrotic cavity containing fibrino-purulent material, compatible with a chronic abscess, was drained and sent for pathological analysis. Estimated blood loss was 900 mL without transfusion, and he remained hemodynamically stable.

Combined drain output was 350 mL of serohematic fluid in the first 24 hours and decreased progressively; drains were removed once output fell below 50 mL in 24 hours. The wound maintained adequate perfusion without signs of ischemia, necrosis, infection, hematoma or fluid collection. Assisted mobilization began on postoperative day 2, with immediate improvements in mobility and local hygiene. Following multidisciplinary reevaluation, the patient regained eligibility for kidney transplantation.

Preoperative appearance of the massive abdominal pannus in a patient with end-stage renal disease and morbid obesity.A) Lateral view demonstrating the severe ptosis, projection, and redundant overhanging tissue that obscured the lower abdominal contour and compromised potential exposure of the iliac fossa required for renal transplantation. caption_evidence.quote:
Figure 3
En-bloc resection of the massive abdominal pannus during extended panniculectomy.The excised specimen measured approximately 110 × 50 cm and weighed 10 kg, illustrating the extent of redundant skin and adipose tissue that created a mechanical barrier to safe iliac fossa exposure for kidney transplantation.
